description: Skillo AI Evaluation Benchmark Corpus — 50 standardised technical interview response pairs

entries.question: How would you design a distributed rate limiter for a high-traffic API gateway serving 1M req/s?
entries.preferred: Use a sliding window counter backed by Redis Sorted Sets with atomic Lua scripts. Store each request timestamp as a ZSET member scored by epoch-ms. ZREMRANGEBYSCORE cleans expired entries; ZCARD returns window cardinality. For cross-region consistency apply Redlock distributed mutex (5 Redis instances, quorum=3). Circuit breaker (50% error threshold, 10s open window) prevents cascade. O(log N) per operation. Fallback: token bucket in local memory with eventual-consistency Gossip sync.
entries.dispreferred: Use Redis to count requests and reset every minute. If the count exceeds the limit, reject the request.

entries.question: Explain the CAP theorem and how it applies to a real-time chat application.
entries.preferred: CAP states a distributed system guarantees only 2 of: Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance. Network partitions are inevitable so we choose CP or AP. For real-time chat choose AP (e.g. Cassandra): messages delivered with potential brief reordering resolved by vector clocks or CRDT ORSets. Use read-repair and hinted handoff for convergence. Conflict resolution: last-write-wins with Lamport timestamps. Tradeoff: user may briefly see stale message order but system stays available.
entries.dispreferred: CAP stands for Consistency, Availability and Partition Tolerance. You can only pick two. For chat I would pick Consistency and Availability.

entries.question: Design a consensus protocol for a distributed key-value store tolerating up to f Byzantine faults.
entries.preferred: Use PBFT requiring 3f+1 nodes. Phases: pre-prepare, prepare, commit. Leader proposes; replicas broadcast prepare messages; commit when 2f+1 prepares received; execute after 2f+1 commits. View-change protocol replaces faulty primary after timeout. For higher throughput use Tendermint BFT (locked-value optimisation, O(n^2) messages). Add BLS threshold signatures to batch validator votes into single constant-size proof.
entries.dispreferred: Use Raft consensus algorithm. It elects a leader and replicates logs to followers. If the leader fails a new election happens.

entries.question: How do you handle exactly-once delivery semantics in a distributed message queue?
entries.preferred: Exactly-once requires idempotent producers and transactional consumers. Kafka: enable idempotent producer (PID + sequence numbers deduplicate retries), use transactions spanning multiple partitions. Consumer: read-process-commit in a single atomic transaction via outbox pattern. Deduplication window: bounded LRU set of message IDs (TTL = max retry window). Dead letter queue for poison messages after N retries.
entries.dispreferred: Use at-least-once delivery and make your consumers idempotent by checking if the message was already processed.

entries.question: Describe how you would implement a distributed transaction spanning multiple microservices.
entries.preferred: Use the Saga pattern. Orchestration: Temporal workflow drives each step and issues compensations on rollback; provides full audit trail. Each step is idempotent (unique idempotency key). Use outbox pattern + CDC (Debezium) for reliable event publishing without XA transactions. 2PC avoided: blocking, prone to coordinator failure in async microservices.
entries.dispreferred: Use two-phase commit (2PC) where a coordinator asks each service to prepare and then commit the transaction.

entries.question: How does consistent hashing work and when would you use virtual nodes?
entries.preferred: Consistent hashing maps both nodes and keys onto a ring (mod 2^32). A key is owned by the first node clockwise. When a node joins or leaves only O(K/N) keys remapped vs O(K) for modular hashing. Virtual nodes: each physical node owns V random ring positions (V=100-150). Benefits: smoother load distribution when capacities differ, faster rebalancing, heterogeneous cluster support. Used in Cassandra and DynamoDB.
entries.dispreferred: Consistent hashing puts servers on a ring and maps each key to the closest server. It reduces the keys that need to move when servers are added or removed.

entries.question: Design a leader election algorithm for a cluster of 7 nodes without a centralized coordinator.
entries.preferred: Use Raft leader election: each node starts as follower with random election timeout (150-300ms). On timeout transitions to candidate, increments term, votes for self, sends RequestVote RPCs. Wins if majority (4/7) grant votes in same term. Heartbeat interval less than election timeout prevents spurious elections. Handles split-vote via randomised backoff. Edge case: network partition causes split-brain prevented by requiring majority quorum for any commit.
entries.dispreferred: Use ZooKeeper for leader election. Nodes register and ZooKeeper picks the leader. If the leader dies, a new one is elected.

entries.question: Explain vector clocks and their role in conflict resolution in eventually consistent systems.
entries.preferred: A vector clock is a list of (nodeId, counter) pairs. On each send, sender increments own counter and attaches full vector. Receiver takes element-wise max and increments own counter. Causality: event A happened-before B iff A vector <= B vector component-wise. Concurrent events are conflicts. Resolution: LWW with wall-clock risk, application-level merge via CRDT, or surface to user. DynamoDB uses vector clocks; Riak uses siblings for concurrent writes.
entries.dispreferred: Vector clocks track the order of events across nodes. Each node has a counter that increments on each event. They help detect conflicts in distributed systems.

entries.question: How would you design a distributed cache with cache invalidation and consistency guarantees?
entries.preferred: Write-through cache: DB and cache updated atomically. Invalidation: CDC (Debezium on Postgres WAL) publishes cache-key invalidation events to Kafka; consumers delete stale keys. Cross-region: cache-aside with TTL as safety net (grace = max replication lag). Thundering herd: probabilistic early expiration with jitter, Redlock on cache miss. Stale-while-revalidate pattern for background refresh. Metrics: cache hit ratio, miss rate, p99 DB fallback latency.
entries.dispreferred: Use Redis as a cache and set a TTL on each key. When the data changes, delete the key from the cache so the next request fetches from the database.

entries.question: Describe the Phi Accrual Failure Detector and how it improves on heartbeat-based failure detection.
entries.preferred: Traditional heartbeat: binary alive/dead at fixed timeout. Phi Accrual uses continuous suspicion level phi derived from inter-arrival time distribution (Gaussian/Exponential). phi = -log10(P_late) where P_late is probability next heartbeat is still outstanding. Callers set own threshold (phi > 8 = 99.99% confidence). Self-adapts to network jitter. Used in Akka Cluster and Cassandra gossip. Edge case: GC pause inflates variance — adaptive window of last N=1000 heartbeats.
entries.dispreferred: Phi Accrual is a failure detector that uses statistics instead of a fixed timeout. It calculates a suspicion level that increases when heartbeats are late.

entries.question: Design a URL shortener service handling 100K writes/day and 10M reads/day.
entries.preferred: Write: hash long URL with MurmurHash3, take 7-char Base62 prefix, check collision via Postgres unique constraint. Store (short_id PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at). Read: Redis cache (short_id to long_url, TTL=24h), 99% hit rate. Cache-aside on miss. CDN edge caching for popular URLs. Scale: read replicas, Redis cluster (16 shards). Analytics: Kafka event stream to ClickHouse for time-series click data. Expiry: pg_cron deletes expired rows nightly.
entries.dispreferred: Use a database to store the long URL and a short code. Generate a random 6-character code and check for duplicates. Use Redis to cache popular URLs.

entries.question: Design a notification system capable of delivering 1M notifications per minute via push, email, and SMS.
entries.preferred: Decouple ingestion from delivery. Ingestion: REST API to Kafka partitioned by user_id. Worker pool consumes and fans-out per channel to separate queues. Push: FCM batch API (500 tokens/call). Email: SES SendBulkTemplatedEmail. SMS: Twilio. Retry: exponential backoff with DLQ after 3 attempts. Idempotency: store notification_id + status in DynamoDB (TTL=7d). Priority lanes: critical notifications via high-priority Kafka partition.
entries.dispreferred: Build an API that sends notifications. Use a queue like SQS to handle bursts. Integrate with Firebase for push, SendGrid for email and Twilio for SMS.

entries.question: Design a search autocomplete system for an e-commerce platform with 50M products.
entries.preferred: Offline: Spark job on product catalog to Elasticsearch with edge n-gram tokenizer (min=1, max=15). Boost by purchase frequency, freshness, inventory status. Online: Nginx to autocomplete service to Redis L1 cache (prefix to top-10, TTL=5min) to Elasticsearch on L1 miss. Debounce 200ms, prefix >= 2 chars. Personalisation: purchase history re-ranks results via BM25 personalised layer. A/B test suggestion diversity. p99 < 50ms target.
entries.dispreferred: Store product names in Elasticsearch and use prefix queries. Cache frequently searched prefixes in Redis. Return the top 10 results sorted by popularity.

entries.question: Design a distributed file storage system similar to Google Drive for 50M users.
entries.preferred: Chunking: files split into 4MB chunks identified by SHA-256 (content-addressing). Deduplication: if chunk hash exists skip upload. Metadata: Postgres stores (file_id, user_id, version, chunk_ids, path). Chunk store: S3 with AES-256 encryption. Upload: parallel chunk upload via pre-signed S3 URLs. CDN for reads. Delta sync: only upload changed chunks. Versioning: retain last 30 versions; soft delete with 30-day trash. Conflict resolution: operational transform or LWW with conflict copy.
entries.dispreferred: Store files in S3 and metadata in a database. Use pre-signed URLs for uploads. Support versioning by keeping old file versions in S3.

entries.question: Design a real-time collaborative text editor for concurrent users.
entries.preferred: Use CRDTs specifically RGA (Replicated Growable Array) for character-level ordering without OT complexity. Each character has unique (siteId, clock) identifier. Insertions and deletions commute regardless of delivery order. Transport: WebSocket server via Elixir Phoenix channels for fan-out. Persistence: append-only operation log in Postgres; periodic snapshots to S3. Awareness: broadcast cursor positions via ephemeral state. Scalability: room-based sharding, one WebSocket server per document with sticky sessions.
entries.dispreferred: Use Operational Transformation like Google Docs. Each operation is transformed against concurrent operations before being applied. Use WebSockets for real-time updates.

entries.question: Design a payment processing system that guarantees exactly-once transaction processing.
entries.preferred: Idempotency key: client generates UUID per payment attempt; server stores (idempotency_key, status, response) in Postgres with unique constraint. State machine: PENDING to PROCESSING to SUCCEEDED or FAILED. Use DB transactions to atomically update status and debit balance (SELECT FOR UPDATE). Saga for multi-step flows with compensating transactions. PCI-DSS scope reduction via card tokenization. Reconciliation: nightly batch compares ledger with processor settlement report.
entries.dispreferred: Use a unique transaction ID to prevent duplicate payments. Store payment status in the database and update it atomically. Use a payment gateway like Stripe.

entries.question: Design a video streaming platform supporting 4K content delivery to 10M concurrent viewers.
entries.preferred: Ingest: transcode via FFmpeg pipeline (H.265, multiple bitrates: 360p/720p/1080p/2160p) to HLS manifests and segments in S3. CDN: CloudFront edge PoPs with geo-routing. ABR: player adjusts quality based on bandwidth (BOLA or Pensieve ML). Manifest server generates personalised manifests (DRM tokens, ad-insertion). Origin shield reduces S3 GET load by 80%. DRM: Widevine and FairPlay via key server. Metrics: rebuffer rate, startup time < 2s, TTFB < 100ms.
entries.dispreferred: Store videos in S3 and use CloudFront CDN for delivery. Transcode videos to multiple resolutions. Use HLS for adaptive bitrate streaming.

entries.question: Design a global leaderboard for an online game with 100M players updated in real time.
entries.preferred: Use Redis Sorted Sets (ZADD O(log N), ZREVRANK O(log N)). Partition by region and game mode to keep each ZSET under 10M members. Real-time: game server to Kafka to leaderboard consumer to Redis ZADD. Persistence: async UPSERT to Postgres every 10s. Read: ZREVRANGE for top-N, ZREVRANK for rank, all O(log N). Pagination: cursor-based via ZREVRANGEBYSCORE. Seasonal reset: RENAME then flush. Tie-breaking: encode score as float (score * 1e9 + MAX_TS - timestamp).
entries.dispreferred: Use Redis Sorted Sets to store player scores. Use ZADD to update scores and ZREVRANK to get the rank. Persist scores to a database periodically.

entries.question: Design a content moderation system that can process 1M images per day using ML.
entries.preferred: Pipeline: upload to S3 event to SQS to moderation worker fleet. Workers call Rekognition or fine-tuned CLIP/ViT to classify (safe/NSFW/violence/spam) with confidence score. Threshold routing: >= 0.95 auto-action; 0.70-0.95 human review; < 0.70 specialist review. Active learning: human decisions feed weekly Sagemaker retraining. PhotoDNA perceptual hash blocks known CSAM. Appeal: rejected content stored 30 days. Metrics: false positive rate < 0.1%, p99 classification latency < 500ms.
entries.dispreferred: Use AWS Rekognition to classify images. Queue images in SQS and process them with Lambda. Send flagged images to human reviewers.

entries.question: Design a ride-sharing dispatch system matching riders to drivers in under 500ms.
entries.preferred: Geospatial: driver locations in Redis GEO (O(log N) radius query). On ride request: GEORADIUS for drivers within 1km ranked by ETA (haversine + traffic factor from cached Distance Matrix API). Match: greedy nearest-available-driver for latency. Lock selected driver atomically (SETNX, 5s TTL). Surge pricing: supply/demand ratio triggers multiplier. Routing: self-hosted OSRM with Contraction Hierarchies for O(1) ETA. SLA: rider-driver match < 500ms p99.
entries.dispreferred: Store driver locations in a database with geospatial indexing. Query nearby drivers when a rider requests a ride. Use Google Maps API for ETA calculation.

entries.question: Explain React reconciliation and how the Fiber architecture improved it.
entries.preferred: Reconciliation: compares virtual DOM trees, applies minimal DOM patches. Key assumptions: different element types trigger full subtree replace; same type updates props; keys identify stable list elements. Fiber (React 16+) replaces recursive stack reconciler with interruptible incremental units of work. Scheduler assigns priority lanes. High-priority updates (user input) interrupt low-priority renders via MessageChannel. useTransition marks updates as non-urgent (transition lane). Time-slicing splits render into <= 5ms chunks preventing jank.
entries.dispreferred: React creates a virtual DOM and compares it with the previous one. Fiber made reconciliation interruptible so high-priority updates can interrupt low-priority ones.

entries.question: How do you architect a micro-frontend system for a large-scale enterprise application?
entries.preferred: Decompose by business domain. Each MFE: own CI/CD, own Webpack/Vite build, own package.json. Integration: Module Federation (Webpack 5) for runtime sharing of React and vendor chunks via dynamic import; or iframes for strongest isolation; or Web Components for framework-agnostic integration. Shell: routing (single-spa), auth token propagation, shared design system via npm. Cross-cutting: shared event bus (BroadcastChannel) for inter-MFE communication. Performance: lazy-loaded on route entry. CSS isolation via Shadow DOM or BEM namespacing.
entries.dispreferred: Use Module Federation to share code between micro-frontends. Each team owns their own MFE and deploys independently. Use a shell app to compose them together.

entries.question: Describe techniques for optimising Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP) in a Next.js application.
entries.preferred: LCP: next/image with priority prop on hero images, serve AVIF/WebP, CDN with correct Cache-Control. SSR/ISR for pre-rendered HTML. CLS: reserve space for dynamic content (explicit width/height, aspect-ratio CSS), avoid inserting DOM above existing content, font-display optional with preloaded font. INP: break long tasks (> 50ms) with scheduler.yield, move heavy computation to Web Workers, startTransition for non-urgent updates, avoid synchronous layout thrashing. Lighthouse CI in GitHub Actions enforces budgets.
entries.dispreferred: Use lazy loading for images, avoid large JavaScript bundles, and preload fonts. Use Next.js Image component and ISR for better performance.

entries.question: Explain the differences between SSR, SSG, ISR, and CSR and when to use each in Next.js.
entries.preferred: CSR: shell HTML hydrated in browser — best for authenticated dashboards; poor SEO, slow LCP. SSR: async Server Components — fresh data per request, good SEO, higher TTFB; use for personalised real-time pages. SSG: generateStaticParams at build time — fastest TTFB via CDN; best for marketing and docs. ISR: stale-while-revalidate with revalidate interval or on-demand revalidateTag; serves cached page while background regeneration runs. Streaming SSR with Suspense: stream HTML chunks for good TTFB with deferred non-critical content.
entries.dispreferred: SSR renders on the server for each request. SSG pre-renders at build time. ISR is SSG with background revalidation. CSR renders in the browser.

entries.question: How do you implement efficient state management at scale with React, avoiding prop drilling and unnecessary re-renders?
entries.preferred: Stratify state: server state (React Query — cache, deduplicate, background refetch), client global state (Zustand or Jotai atoms — fine-grained subscriptions), local UI state (useState co-located). Avoid prop drilling: React Context for cross-cutting concerns in small contexts to limit re-render scope. Performance: memo and useCallback for referential stability; useMemo for derived computations; React.lazy for code-splitting. Concurrent: useTransition for non-urgent updates keeps UI responsive. XState for complex async flows prevents impossible states.
entries.dispreferred: Use Redux for global state and React Context for lighter shared state. Use React.memo and useCallback to prevent unnecessary re-renders.

entries.question: How would you design a design system that scales across multiple products and teams?
entries.preferred: Token-driven: design tokens (color, spacing, typography, elevation) in Style Dictionary compiled to CSS custom properties and JS/TS exports. Component library: React + TypeScript, Storybook for isolated development, Chromatic for visual regression on every PR. Versioning: semver with Conventional Commits and semantic-release. Distribution: private npm registry. Governance: RFC process for new components, design-dev a11y review pairing. Testing: jest + testing-library, axe-core for accessibility, Percy for visual snapshots. Adoption: track package version distribution across consuming apps.
entries.dispreferred: Create a component library with reusable React components. Use Storybook to document them. Publish to npm and version with semver.

entries.question: Describe how you would architect the caching strategy for a React SPA fetching data from multiple REST APIs.
entries.preferred: React Query as server-state cache. Configure staleTime (30s for reference data, 0 for real-time) and cacheTime (5min for inactive entries). React Query coalesces concurrent requests for same key. Optimistic updates: useMutation with onMutate/onError/onSettled for instant feedback and rollback. Prefetching: queryClient.prefetchQuery on hover. Background refetch: refetchOnWindowFocus. HTTP layer: axios interceptors for auth headers, retry with exponential backoff. Service Worker (Workbox): stale-while-revalidate for static assets, network-first for API calls.
entries.dispreferred: Use React Query to cache API calls with staleTime and cacheTime. Implement optimistic updates for mutations. Add retry logic for failed requests.

entries.question: How do you implement accessibility (a11y) at scale in a component library?
entries.preferred: Follow WCAG 2.1 AA. ARIA: use semantic HTML first, add aria-label when native label insufficient, aria-live regions for dynamic content. Keyboard: all interactive elements Tab-reachable, Enter/Space activates, Escape dismisses modals. Focus management: useRef + focus() after modal open, focus trap inside dialogs (focus-trap-react). Colour contrast: 4.5:1 normal text verified via axe-core. Motion: prefers-reduced-motion disables animations. Testing: @testing-library/user-event for keyboard, jest-axe for violations, manual screen reader testing (NVDA + Firefox). Include a11y in PR checklist.
entries.dispreferred: Add aria labels to all interactive elements. Test with a screen reader. Ensure colour contrast meets WCAG standards. Make all components keyboard navigable.

entries.question: Explain how the browser event loop, microtask queue, and macrotask queue work and how they affect React rendering.
entries.preferred: Call stack executes synchronous JS. Macrotask queue: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, MessageChannel. Microtask queue: Promise.then, queueMicrotask — drained completely after each macrotask before next render. React 18 Concurrent: uses MessageChannel for Scheduler to yield between render chunks. useTransition defers state update to low-priority scheduler lane. setState inside event handlers is batched in same macrotask. async setState also batched in React 18 (flushSync forces synchronous flush). Long sync tasks block rendering — split with scheduler.yield.
entries.dispreferred: The event loop processes tasks from the task queue one at a time. Promises use the microtask queue which runs before the next task. React batches setState calls inside event handlers.

entries.question: How do you prevent and detect memory leaks in a long-running React single-page application?
entries.preferred: Common causes: uncleared event listeners, uncleared timers, stale closures retaining large objects, abandoned async operations setting state on unmounted components. Prevention: useEffect cleanup removes subscriptions, timers, and fetch calls (AbortController on unmount). Detection: Chrome DevTools Memory tab — Heap Snapshot before/after suspect action, compare retained size; Allocation Timeline for growing allocation sites. React DevTools Profiler for unnecessary re-renders. Automated: puppeteer-based memory test (heap before/after 50 navigation cycles). Budget alert if JS heap > 200MB via RUM.
entries.dispreferred: Clean up event listeners and timers in useEffect return functions. Use AbortController to cancel fetch requests when a component unmounts. Profile with Chrome DevTools to find memory leaks.

entries.question: How would you implement an infinite scroll virtualized list in React from scratch without third-party libraries?
entries.preferred: Compute total virtual container height as itemCount * itemHeight. Attach an onScroll listener (or IntersectionObserver on sentinel boundaries) with requestAnimationFrame throttle. Derive visible start index as Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / itemHeight) - overscan) and end index as Math.min(itemCount - 1, Math.ceil((scrollTop + viewportHeight) / itemHeight) + overscan). Render only slice(startIndex, endIndex + 1) absolutely positioned with transform: translateY(index * itemHeight) to leverage GPU compositing and prevent reflows. Recycle DOM nodes and preserve key stability.
entries.dispreferred: Listen to the window scroll event and append more items to the state array when user reaches the bottom of the page.

entries.question: How do you optimize bundle size and achieve sub-second TTI in a modern single page application?
entries.preferred: Employ Route-based and Component-level code splitting using React.lazy and dynamic import(). Analyze bundles via webpack-bundle-analyzer to eliminate duplicate dependencies and heavy libraries (replace moment with date-fns/dayjs or native Intl). Configure tree-shaking with ES modules and sideEffects: false in package.json. Implement Brotli/Gzip compression on CDN edge with aggressive Cache-Control: immutable for hashed chunks. Offload non-critical telemetry and polyfills to dynamic runtime loaders or Web Workers.
entries.dispreferred: Minify your JS code, enable Gzip on your server, and use React.lazy to split routes.

entries.question: Explain how WebSockets and Server-Sent Events (SSE) differ and when you would choose one over the other in frontend architecture.
entries.preferred: WebSockets provide bi-directional, full-duplex TCP communication over a single connection with low framing overhead (2-10 bytes), ideal for real-time collaborative editing (CRDT sync), gaming, and bidirectional chat. SSE provides unidirectional server-to-client streaming over standard HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, natively supporting automatic reconnections, event IDs, and standard HTTP proxy/auth/firewall traversal with text/event-stream. Choose SSE for financial tickers, live log streaming, and LLM token generation where client-to-server traffic uses standard POST endpoints.
entries.dispreferred: WebSockets are two-way and SSE is one-way from server to client. Use WebSockets for chat and SSE for simple notifications.

entries.question: How would you design a client-side offline-first architecture with background synchronization?
entries.preferred: Service Worker intercepts fetch requests implementing Cache-First or Stale-While-Revalidate strategies via Cache Storage API. Application data persisted in IndexedDB using Dexie or idb wrappers. Local mutations appended to an IndexedDB outbox queue with optimistic UI updates. When navigator.onLine fires or Service Worker receives a SyncEvent (Background Sync API), queue drains sequentially with idempotency keys. Conflicts resolved via server timestamps or CRDTs. Failed mutations retry with exponential backoff before routing to user error queues.
entries.dispreferred: Use localStorage to save user changes when offline, listen to the online event, and post the data to the API when connection is restored.

entries.question: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and what defense-in-depth strategies prevent it in React applications?
entries.preferred: XSS occurs when malicious scripts inject into web applications (Stored, Reflected, DOM-based). React inherently escapes JSX string interpolations, mitigating basic injection. Defense-in-depth: 1) Strict Content Security Policy (CSP) header (script-src 'self' 'nonce-...', object-src 'none', base-uri 'self') preventing inline eval/scripts. 2) Never bypass JSX without DOMPurify sanitization (avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML). 3) Validate URLs before href/src insertion against javascript: schemes. 4) Set HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookies preventing session token theft via document.cookie.
entries.dispreferred: React automatically escapes inputs so XSS is not a big issue. Avoid using dangerouslySetInnerHTML and sanitize inputs with regex.

entries.question: How would you design an end-to-end real-time recommendation system serving 50M daily active users?
entries.preferred: Two-stage pipeline: Retrieval and Ranking. Retrieval (Candidate Generation): Two-tower neural network (User Tower + Item Tower) trained on co-visitation/engagement logs, generating 128-d embeddings. Index items in vector database (FAISS/HNSW or Milvus) for sub-10ms Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search, retrieving top 500 candidates. Ranking: Multi-task ranking model (MMoE or DeepFM) predicting pCTR and pCVR on candidate features, real-time context (device, time), and user sequence features from low-latency feature store (Feast/Redis). Re-ranking: Apply business logic, diversity filtering (maximal marginal relevance), and frequency capping.
entries.dispreferred: Use collaborative filtering to find similar users and recommend items they liked. Rank results using logistic regression.

entries.question: How do you detect and mitigate data drift and concept drift in production machine learning pipelines?
entries.preferred: Data Drift (P(X) changes): monitor feature distributions against training baseline using Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for continuous features and Population Stability Index (PSI) or Wasserstein Distance. PSI > 0.2 indicates significant shift. Concept Drift (P(Y|X) changes): track online evaluation metrics (pCTR vs observed CTR calibration, F1, log-loss) via sliding time windows. Detection toolchain: Evidently AI or Great Expectations integrated with Prometheus/Grafana. Mitigation: automated retraining triggers on drift thresholds, exponential decay weighting on older training data, and shadow/canary deployments.
entries.dispreferred: Check if model accuracy drops over time in Grafana. If it does, retrain the model with fresh data from the last month.

entries.question: Explain the architectural difference between LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) and full fine-tuning for Large Language Models.
entries.preferred: Full fine-tuning updates all model parameters W_0 in R^(d x k), requiring optimizer states (AdamW stores 8 bytes/param) and full gradient checkpoints, demanding massive GPU VRAM (e.g., >160GB for 70B in 16-bit) and producing complete weight checkpoints per task. LoRA freezes W_0 and injects trainable rank-decomposition matrices A in R^(r x k) and B in R^(d x r) where Delta W = B * A with rank r << min(d, k) (typically r=8 to 64) scaled by alpha/r. Memory footprint reduced by up to 75%, zero inference latency overhead when weights merged, and enables serving multiple task adapters on a single base model.
entries.dispreferred: LoRA only tunes a small percentage of model weights instead of the whole model so it uses much less memory and trains faster.

entries.question: How would you build a low-latency LLM serving pipeline supporting high-concurrency inference?
entries.preferred: Utilize vLLM or TensorRT-LLM with PagedAttention to eliminate memory fragmentation in KV cache, managing KV blocks as virtual memory pages. Implement Continuous (Iteration-level) Batching instead of request-level padding. Apply weight quantization: AWQ or FP8 for minimal perplexity degradation with 2x throughput. For multi-GPU: Tensor Parallelism (Megatron-LM style) within a node, Pipeline Parallelism across nodes. Deploy speculative decoding with a draft model for 2-3x token generation speedup. Monitor TTFT (Time to First Token) and TPOT (Time Per Output Token).
entries.dispreferred: Run the model with HuggingFace Transformers on a fast GPU and use FastAPI with Uvicorn to handle concurrent requests.

entries.question: Explain the bias-variance tradeoff and how regularization techniques (L1, L2, Dropout) address overfitting.
entries.preferred: Total expected error decomposes into Bias^2 + Variance + Irreducible Noise. High bias stems from overly simplistic models (underfitting); high variance stems from model sensitivity to training noise (overfitting). Regularization controls model capacity: L2 (Ridge/Weight Decay) adds lambda * ||w||_2^2 penalty to loss, shrinking weights towards zero smoothly and preventing reliance on single features. L1 (Lasso) adds lambda * ||w||_1 penalty, producing sparse weights due to diamond constraint geometry, acting as feature selector. Dropout randomly zeroes activations with probability p during training, preventing co-adaptation of neurons and approximating an ensemble of 2^N sub-networks.
entries.dispreferred: Bias is when the model is too simple and variance is when it overfits. L1 makes weights zero, L2 shrinks weights, and Dropout turns off neurons randomly.

entries.question: How would you architect a Feature Store for real-time ML inference and offline training?
entries.preferred: Dual-storage architecture maintaining training-serving consistency. Offline store: Snowflake/BigQuery or Parquet on S3 optimized for high-throughput batch writes and point-in-time correct (time-travel) feature joins to prevent data leakage during backtesting. Online store: Redis or DynamoDB with sub-10ms key-value lookups indexed by entity_id. Streaming ingestion: Kafka/Flink streaming engine calculates rolling window aggregations (e.g., 10-minute transaction count) and dual-writes to online and offline stores. Centralized registry (Feast/Hopsworks) defines feature schemas, data types, and SLA lineage.
entries.dispreferred: Save features in Postgres for training and cache them in Redis so the API can read them quickly during prediction.

entries.question: Explain how Self-Attention works in Transformer models and derive its computational complexity.
entries.preferred: Given input representations X in R^(N x d), project linearly to Queries Q = X*W_Q, Keys K = X*W_K, and Values V = X*W_V. Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q*K^T / sqrt(d_k)) * V. Q*K^T computes pairwise dot-product compatibility matrix in R^(N x N), scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k) to prevent vanishing gradients in softmax for large d_k. Computational complexity: Q*K^T takes O(N^2 * d) operations; Softmax * V takes O(N^2 * d). Overall time and memory complexity is O(N^2 * d) with respect to sequence length N. Mitigations for long context include FlashAttention (tiling IO-aware kernel) and Linear/Sparse Attention.
entries.dispreferred: Self-attention computes dot products between queries and keys, passes through softmax, and multiplies by values. The complexity is O(N squared).

entries.question: How do you evaluate and mitigate hallucinations and toxic outputs in an enterprise RAG system?
entries.preferred: Evaluation: Multi-metric Ragas or TruLens framework tracking: 1) Faithfulness (is the answer grounded in context?), 2) Answer Relevance, 3) Context Precision. Implement LLM-as-a-judge with contrastive rubrics. Mitigation: Retrieval guardrails: minimum cosine similarity threshold, re-ranking with cross-encoders (BGE-Reranker) to filter irrelevant chunks. Prompt engineering: strict negative constraints ('Answer only using context, if unknown reply UNKNOWN'). Generation guardrails: NeMo Guardrails or Llama Guard for toxicity classification. Post-generation citation verification: string/semantic alignment between output claims and source chunk offsets.
entries.dispreferred: Use a good prompt telling the model not to lie. Check answers with another prompt and set temperature to 0 to prevent hallucinations.

entries.question: Tell me about a time you had to resolve a major architectural disagreement with another senior engineer.
entries.preferred: Situation: At my previous company, our team was split on migrating our core processing pipeline to microservices vs modular monolith. Task: As tech lead, I needed to resolve the deadlock and deliver the Q3 scalability milestone without team friction. Action: I scheduled an objective benchmarking spike. Instead of debating philosophies, we defined 4 measurable criteria: p99 latency under 10k RPS, deployment independence, developer onboarding time, and operational cost. Both engineers built a 2-day prototype. When data showed the modular monolith beat latency by 3x and reduced infrastructure cost by 40%, we unanimously aligned on it. Result: Delivered on time, zero production incidents during Black Friday, and established our team's RFC decision framework.
entries.dispreferred: I had an argument with an engineer about microservices. I called a meeting, discussed our points of view, and we agreed to go with my suggestion because it was simpler.

entries.question: Describe a situation where a critical production outage occurred under your watch. How did you handle it?
entries.preferred: Situation: At 2 PM on a Tuesday, our payment checkout service threw 503 errors for 35% of traffic following a canary deployment. Task: As the incident commander, my priority was immediate mitigation to stop customer impact, followed by root-cause diagnosis. Action: I immediately executed an automated rollback to the previous stable release within 4 minutes, restoring availability. Concurrently, I assigned roles: one engineer on log triage, one drafting status updates for support, and myself coordinating communications. Root cause analysis revealed an unindexed database migration caused connection pool exhaustion. Result: Restored 100% availability in 6 minutes. Post-mortem produced an automated CI gate requiring EXPLAIN plans on all migration PRs and synthetic canary load tests.
entries.dispreferred: A deployment broke production. I noticed the error rate spike, rolled back the change right away, and fixed the bug in the code before redeploying.

entries.question: Tell me about a time you had to deliver a high-stakes project under an unrealistic deadline.
entries.preferred: Situation: Executive leadership committed to launching a partner integration in 6 weeks when initial engineering estimates projected 14 weeks. Task: As the lead engineer, I had to prevent team burnout while delivering a secure, functional v1 to meet contractual commitments. Action: I led a scope negotiation workshop using MoSCoW prioritization with product and partner teams. We deselect non-critical automated admin workflows in favor of audited internal tools, reducing scope by 50%. We adopted proven off-the-shelf auth (OAuth2 with Auth0) instead of custom identity. I instituted daily 15-minute risk blockers and paired junior engineers with senior leads. Result: Shipped core integration 3 days ahead of deadline with zero P0 security vulnerabilities, enabling a $2M enterprise partnership.
entries.dispreferred: We had a strict deadline, so the team worked overtime and weekends. I made sure everyone stayed focused and we successfully delivered on time.

entries.question: Give an example of how you mentored a struggling junior or mid-level engineer to improve their performance.
entries.preferred: Situation: A junior engineer on my team was missing sprint commitments and receiving frequent rework requests on PRs due to edge-case bugs. Task: Help them build confidence, improve code quality, and reach independence without micromanagement. Action: Rather than pointing out flaws, I instituted weekly 1-on-1 pairing sessions. We analyzed their PR feedback together and identified that requirements were being coded before edge cases were mapped. I introduced them to Test-Driven Development (TDD), encouraging them to write failing unit tests for error boundaries first. I also had them shadow my code reviews on complex PRs. Result: Within two quarters, their PR cycle time dropped from 4.2 days to 1.1 days, rework rates fell by 70%, and they were promoted to mid-level engineer.
entries.dispreferred: I noticed a junior developer was struggling with code quality. I reviewed their PRs more carefully, showed them the right way to write code, and they improved.

entries.question: Tell me about a time you made a significant mistake or bad technical decision. How did you handle the aftermath?
entries.preferred: Situation: Early in my career, I chose a NoSQL document database for an inventory management service because of rapid initial prototyping speed. Task: As the business expanded into multi-warehouse reservation and auditing, the lack of ACID multi-document transactions caused ghost inventory anomalies. Action: I owned the mistake transparently in our engineering retrospective rather than blaming requirements churn. I proposed a phased remediation plan: built a reconciliation daemon to detect inconsistencies immediately, then designed a zero-downtime dual-write migration to PostgreSQL with row-level locks. I led the migration over 3 sprints without downtime. Result: Eliminated inventory discrepancies completely and published a post-mortem guide on storage engine trade-offs for the organization.
entries.dispreferred: I picked the wrong database for a project and it couldn't handle relational data later on. I admitted my mistake and migrated the data to SQL.

entries.question: Describe a situation where you had to influence a product manager or stakeholder without formal authority.
entries.preferred: Situation: Product management prioritized 5 new user-facing features over addressing severe technical debt in our checkout caching layer, which had a p99 latency of 1.8s. Task: Convince the PM to allocate 30% of sprint capacity to refactoring without formal executive authority. Action: Instead of arguing technical elegance, I translated latency into business metrics: cited internal analytics showing a 100ms latency increase correlated to a 1.2% drop in conversion ($150k monthly loss). I proposed a timeboxed 1-sprint refactoring spike with agreed KPI targets. Result: The PM approved the allocation. We reduced p99 latency from 1.8s to 240ms, resulting in a measurable 4.5% conversion uplift ($540k annual recurring revenue), earning engineering leadership commendation.
entries.dispreferred: The PM wanted new features but we had technical debt. I explained to them why clean code is important and convinced them to give us time to refactor.

entries.question: Tell me about a time you took the initiative to improve an engineering process or developer experience across teams.
entries.preferred: Situation: CI build and test pipelines took 42 minutes across 6 repository microservices, causing developer frustration and slow deployment velocity. Task: Reduce CI turnaround time to under 10 minutes organization-wide as a self-directed initiative. Action: I profiled the GitHub Actions workflows and identified bottlenecks: un-cached Docker layer rebuilds and sequential Jest execution. I implemented Nx distributed task execution with remote cloud caching, containerized test runners, and parallelized test sharding across 4 runners. I created reusable GitHub Actions composite workflows and documented the setup in an internal engineering RFC. Result: Cut CI duration from 42 minutes to 7.5 minutes (82% reduction), saving an estimated 140 developer hours weekly and accelerating daily production deployments by 3x.
entries.dispreferred: Our build times were very slow, so I updated GitHub Actions to run tests in parallel and enabled caching, which made the builds much faster for everyone.
